definition: Cognitive models of information retrieval rest on the mix of areas such as cognitive science, human-computer interaction, information retrieval, and library science.
details: They describe the relationship between a person's cognitive model of the information sought and the organization of this information in an information system. These models attempt to understand how a person is searching for information so that the database and the search of this database can be designed in such a way as to best serve the user. Information retrieval may incorporate multiple tasks and cognitive problems, particularly because different people may have different methods for attempting to find this information and expect the information to be in different forms. Cognitive models of information retrieval may be attempts at something as apparently prosaic as improving search results or may be something more complex, such as attempting to create a database which can be queried with natural language search.

explainer.lead: Cognitive models of information retrieval focus on how people think about what they need, how they search, and what form they expect answers to take. They help designers organize information systems and searches around those human differences rather than assuming everyone searches in the same way.

tiers.eli5: Imagine two people looking through the same cookbook: one wants a quick dinner, while the other wants to learn why bread rises. A good information system notices that people can have different goals and want different kinds of answers. This idea helps designers arrange information and search tools so both people can find what they need more easily.
tiers.practitioner: Apply the approach by treating the user's task, search strategy, and expected information format as inputs to database organization and search-interface design. It can guide comparatively direct work such as improving search results, as well as more ambitious systems that accept natural-language queries. A central pitfall is designing for one assumed search process when users may approach the same retrieval task differently.
tiers.paperLevel: The approach describes the relation R(U, O), where U is a person's cognitive model of the information sought and O is the organization of that information in an information system. Its aim is to understand search behavior so that both the database and its search process can better serve the user. A key difficulty is that retrieval can involve multiple tasks and cognitive problems, with users employing different strategies and expecting different representations of information.

explainer.example: Two users search a health database for information about knee pain. One expects a short practical explanation, while the other expects detailed research material; a cognitively informed design would account for these different tasks and expected forms rather than treating identical queries as identical information needs.

usedIn.name: Search-system design
usedIn.detail: Uses models of how people seek information to improve search results.

usedIn.name: Database design
usedIn.detail: Aligns the organization of stored information and database search with users' needs.

usedIn.name: Natural-language querying
usedIn.detail: Supports the more complex goal of databases that people can query using natural language.

usedIn.name: Library and information science
usedIn.detail: Connects human information-seeking behavior with the organization of information systems.

explainer.intuition: A search is not just a match between words and records: it begins with a person's mental picture of what they need. Retrieval works better when the system's organization and search process take that picture, the person's task, and their preferred form of information into account.
howItWorks: Identify the information the person is seeking and the task surrounding the search.
Describe the person's cognitive model of that need and their way of searching.
Compare this with how the information system organizes and presents its contents.
Design the database and search process to reduce the gap between the two.
explainer.whyItMatters: It gives designers a way to address differences in search strategies, tasks, and expected information formats. That perspective can guide both ordinary improvements to search results and more complex goals such as natural-language database search.
misconceptions: It is not solely a technique for ranking search results.
It does not assume that all users search in the same way.
It concerns both the database's organization and the process of searching it.
